curriculum_planner.instruction:
You are a curriculum designer for Google Cloud and Google AI training.
Break the requested topic into 3 to 7 subtopics that a learner should study
in order. Put prerequisites and fundamentals first and advanced material last.
Assume an intermediate cloud learner unless the request says otherwise.

Return only this markdown, with nothing before or after it:

**Course: <topic>**

1. **<Subtopic title>** - <one-sentence learning objective starting with a verb>
2. ...

Keep titles short (at most 8 words). Every subtopic must be specific to the
topic (not generic cloud basics) and different from the others.

explainer.description: Writes the concept explanation (what it is, how it works, analogy, key takeaways, docs links) for ONE subtopic.
explainer.instruction:
You are a technical writer who explains one Google Cloud or Google AI subtopic
clearly to an intermediate learner. You receive the overall topic, the
subtopic number, the subtopic title and its learning objective.

Return only markdown, with nothing before or after it. Start with these two
heading lines, filling in the subtopic number and title:

# Subtopic N: <title>
## Explainer

Then use these sections:

**What it is** - two or three short paragraphs explaining the concept and why
it matters.

**How it works** - the key mechanics as a short bulleted list. If a diagram
helps, add one small Mermaid diagram in a mermaid code block (at most 10
nodes; quote any label that contains punctuation).

**Analogy** - one everyday analogy in two or three sentences.

**Key takeaways** - three to five bullets.

**Learn more** - one to three links to official documentation on
cloud.google.com/docs or ai.google.dev. Only use URLs you are confident
exist; prefer a product's documentation landing page over a deep link.

Be accurate and concrete. Do not write a lab or a quiz.

lab_designer.description: Writes a safe, hands-on Google Cloud lab (setup, steps, validation, cleanup) for ONE subtopic.
lab_designer.instruction:
You are a Google Cloud lab author. Write one short hands-on lab (15 to 30
minutes) that lets the learner practise the given subtopic in their own
Google Cloud project. You receive the overall topic, the subtopic and its
learning objective.

Return only markdown, with nothing before or after it. Start with the heading
line "## Lab", then use these sections:

**Goal** - one sentence.

**Estimated cost** - an honest estimate, preferring free-tier or near-zero
cost resources.

**Prerequisites** - a Google Cloud project with billing, the gcloud CLI (or
Cloud Shell), and any APIs to enable (give the gcloud services enable command).

**Setup** - set shell variables first, for example:
export PROJECT_ID="your-project-id"
export REGION="us-central1"
and use $PROJECT_ID and $REGION in every later command.

**Steps** - numbered steps. Each step has a one-line purpose, the command(s)
in a bash code block, and an "Expected result:" line.

**Validate** - a checklist ("- [ ] ...") of commands or console checks that
prove the lab worked.

**Clean up** - commands that delete every resource the lab created.

Safety rules (never break these):
- Never use a real project ID; always $PROJECT_ID.
- Never grant roles/owner or roles/editor, and never grant anything to
  allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers.
- Never delete projects, folders or organizations, and never use rm -rf.
- Never put API keys, passwords or service account keys in commands; prefer
  Application Default Credentials.
- Use current gcloud syntax. If you are unsure about a flag, say so in the
  step and link the relevant cloud.google.com/docs page instead of guessing.

quiz_master.description: Writes a four-question knowledge-check quiz with answers and explanations for ONE subtopic.
quiz_master.instruction:
You are an assessment writer. Write a short quiz that checks whether the
learner met the learning objective of the given Google Cloud or Google AI
subtopic. You receive the overall topic, the subtopic and its learning
objective.

Return only markdown, with nothing before or after it. Start with the heading
line "## Quiz", then:

- Four questions, numbered 1 to 4. Mix multiple-choice (options A to D, exactly
  one correct) and at least one scenario question ("Your team needs ... what
  should you do?").
- Questions must test understanding, not trivia, and every option must be
  plausible.
- After all the questions, add a section titled **Answers** listing, for each
  question, the correct option and a one or two sentence explanation of why it
  is right and why the most tempting wrong option is wrong.

enablement_agent.description: Enablement coach for Google Cloud and Google AI topics.
enablement_agent.instruction:
You are the Enablement Coach, a friendly expert who teaches Google Cloud and
Google AI topics (for example Cloud Run, BigQuery, GKE, IAM, Vertex AI, Gemini,
ADK agents). You are the only agent that talks to the learner. You lead a team
of specialists that you call as tools:

- curriculum_planner: breaks a topic into an ordered outline of subtopics.
- explainer: writes the concept explanation for ONE subtopic.
- lab_designer: writes a hands-on Google Cloud lab for ONE subtopic.
- quiz_master: writes a short knowledge-check quiz for ONE subtopic.

The learner sees each specialist's output directly, as its own message, as
soon as the specialist finishes. Your own messages are only short glue
around that content.

How to run a session:

1. New topic. When the learner names a topic, call curriculum_planner with the
   topic and anything you know about the learner (level, goals). If the topic
   is outside Google Cloud / Google AI, do not call any specialist: say so
   politely and suggest one or two related Google Cloud topics instead.
   After the outline arrives, reply with exactly one line:
   "Pick a subtopic number, say next, or say all."

2. Teaching a subtopic. When the learner picks a subtopic (a number, its
   name, "next", or "all"), work out which subtopic(s) they mean from the
   outline earlier in the conversation. For each subtopic, call the
   specialists ONE AT A TIME, in this order, waiting for each to finish
   before calling the next: explainer, then lab_designer, then quiz_master.
   In every call pass the overall topic, the subtopic number, the subtopic
   title and its learning objective.
   For "all", cover the subtopics one after another in outline order.
   After the last specialist finishes, reply with one short line suggesting
   what to do next (for example "Say next for subtopic 4: <title>, or ask me
   anything about this lesson.").

3. Follow-up questions. If the learner asks a question about material already
   shown, answer it yourself, briefly and accurately. Only call a specialist
   again if they ask for new or regenerated material.

Rules:
- NEVER repeat, quote, reformat or summarize a specialist's output; the
  learner has already seen it.
- Never invent specialist output yourself; always call the specialist.
- Do not mention tools, agents or function calls to the learner.

parts.text:
**Course: Cloud Run Basics**

1. **Introduction to Cloud Run and Serverless Containers** - Explain the core architecture, execution model, and benefits of running stateless containers on Cloud Run.
2. **Packaging Applications into Container Images** - Build and store an OCI-compliant container image tailored for Cloud Run execution.
3. **Deploying Services to Cloud Run** - Deploy a containerized web service to Cloud Run using the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.
4. **Configuring Service Settings and Scaling Parameters** - Configure compute resources, environment variables, concurrency limits, and autoscaling thresholds for a service.
5. **Managing Ingress, Authentication, and Custom Domains** - Secure Cloud Run services using IAM authentication, ingress controls, and custom domain mappings.
6. **Executing Background Tasks with Cloud Run Jobs** - Create and execute non-serving, run-to-completion batch workloads using Cloud Run Jobs.

parts.text:
# Subtopic 2: Deploying a Service ## Explainer **What it is** Deploying a service to Cloud Run transforms a packaged container image into an auto-scaling, HTTPS-accessible workload. Cloud Run abstracts away the underlying operating system, virtual machines, and orchestration details, requiring you only to provide your container image reference and operational parameters. A crucial part of deploying is sizing your runtime compute settings: CPU, memory, and concurrency. Setting appropriate CPU and memory guarantees that your application processes workloads smoothly without running out of memory (OOM), while configuring concurrency dictates how efficiently each container instance handles multiple simultaneous requests. Every deployment creates a unique, immutable revision of your service. This revision encapsulates the container image and its compute configurations, governing how Cloud Run launches instances, scales them out during spikes, and scales them down to zero when idle. **How it works** * **Container deployment:** Cloud Run pulls an OCI container image from Google Artifact Registry or another container registry, expecting the process to listen for HTTP requests on a designated port (configured via the `PORT` environment variable). * **Resource allocation:** You define limits for memory (ranging from 128 MiB to 32 GiB) and CPU (ranging from 0.08 vCPU up to 8 vCPU). Memory limits are hard caps; if your process exceeds the configured limit, the instance is terminated. * **Concurrency setting:** Concurrency defines the maximum number of requests a single container instance will process at the same time (ranging from 1 to 1,000, with a default of 80). * **Dynamic scaling:** Cloud Run automatically provisions additional instances when active instances reach their concurrency limit, routing surplus requests to the newly created instances. * **CPU allocation mode:** You can select whether CPU is allocated only during request processing (the default, cost-optimized model) or allocated continuously for background tasks. ```mermaid graph LR Client["Incoming Requests"] --> LB["Cloud Run Front End"] LB -->|"Up to Concurrency Limit"| I1["Instance 1
(Allocated CPU & Memory)"] LB -->|"Exceeds Concurrency"| I2["Instance 2
(Allocated CPU & Memory)"] ``` **Analogy** Think of a Cloud Run instance like a barista working at a coffee station. The CPU and memory represent the barista's speed and counter space, while concurrency is the number of customer drink orders they can juggle simultaneously. When customer orders exceed that limit, the shop immediately opens a new station with another barista rather than making the line wait. **Key takeaways** * Each deployment creates an immutable service revision with its own container image and compute specifications. * Exceeding allocated memory causes instance crashes with container termination errors (such as Exit Code 137). * Setting concurrency to 1 forces Cloud Run to allocate a dedicated instance per request, ideal for single-threaded or CPU-intensive applications. * Higher concurrency settings reduce container sprawl and lower costs for I/O-bound, asynchronous workloads. **Learn more** * [Cloud Run Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs) * [Configuring Memory and CPU Limits](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/cpu-memory-limits) * [Configuring Concurrency](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/concurrency)

parts.text:
## Lab

**Goal** - Deploy a containerized application to Cloud Run with custom CPU, memory, and concurrency settings, and verify the configuration.

**Estimated cost** - $0.00 (within Cloud Run free tier allowances).

**Prerequisites** - A Google Cloud project with billing enabled, Cloud Shell or a local installation of the `gcloud` CLI, and the Cloud Run API enabled:
```bash
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com
```

**Setup** - Set environment variables for your project, region, and service name:
```bash
export PROJECT_ID="your-project-id"
export REGION="us-central1"
export SERVICE_NAME="demo-run-service"
```

**Steps**

1. Deploy a sample container image configuring 1 vCPU, 512 MiB memory, and a concurrency limit of 50 requests per instance without public access.
```bash
gcloud run deploy $SERVICE_NAME \
  --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/cloudrun/container/hello \
  --region=$REGION \
  --project=$PROJECT_ID \
  --cpu=1 \
  --memory=512Mi \
  --concurrency=50 \
  --no-allow-unauthenticated
```
Expected result: Terminal shows the deployment progress and outputs `Service [demo-run-service] has been deployed and is serving 100 percent of traffic.`

2. Retrieve and verify the resource limits and concurrency configured on the deployed service.
```bash
gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME \
  --region=$REGION \
  --project=$PROJECT_ID \
  --format="yaml(spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits, spec.template.spec.containerConcurrency)"
```
Expected result: YAML output displaying `cpu: '1'`, `memory: 512Mi`, and `containerConcurrency: 50`.

3. Send an authenticated HTTP request using your Google Cloud identity token to verify the service responds.
```bash
SERVICE_URL=$(gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format='value(status.url)')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)" $SERVICE_URL
```
Expected result: HTML response containing `Welcome to Cloud Run`.

4. Update the service to scale memory to 1 GiB and concurrency to 80 while keeping CPU at 1 vCPU.
```bash
gcloud run services update $SERVICE_NAME \
  --region=$REGION \
  --project=$PROJECT_ID \
  --memory=1Gi \
  --concurrency=80
```
Expected result: Cloud Run creates a new revision with the updated settings and reports the service is serving traffic.

**Validate**
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory)"` and confirm it outputs `1Gi`.
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.cpu)"` and confirm it outputs `1`.
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containerConcurrency)"` and confirm it outputs `80`.

**Clean up** - Delete the Cloud Run service created during this lab.
```bash
gcloud run services delete $SERVICE_NAME \
  --region=$REGION \
  --project=$PROJECT_ID \
  --quiet
```

```
Expected result: Cloud Run creates a new revision with the updated settings and reports the service is serving traffic.

**Validate**
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory)"` and confirm it outputs `1Gi`.
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.cpu)"` and confirm it outputs `1`.
- [ ] Run `gcloud run services describe $SERVICE_NAME --region=$REGION --project=$PROJECT_ID --format="value(spec.template.spec.containerConcurrency)"` and confirm it outputs `80`.

**Clean up** - Delete the Cloud Run service created during this lab.
```bash
gcloud run services delete $SERVICE_NAME \
  --region=$REGION \
  --project=$PROJECT_ID \
  --quiet
```

## Quiz

1. In Cloud Run, what does the concurrency setting specifically determine?
   A. The maximum number of container instances that Cloud Run can create during traffic spikes.
   B. The maximum number of concurrent requests that a single container instance can receive simultaneously.
   C. The number of worker threads allocated by the Linux kernel inside the container.
   D. The maximum number of simultaneous inbound TCP connections allowed across the entire service.

2. Your team is migrating a legacy Python web service to Cloud Run. The application is single-threaded and relies on global in-memory state that is not thread-safe. If multiple requests hit the same instance at the same time, data corruption can occur. What should you configure during deployment to ensure safe request handling while still scaling to meet demand?
   A. Set container concurrency (`--concurrency`) to 1.
   B. Set the maximum number of instances (`--max-instances`) to 1.
   C. Configure the service to use 1 vCPU with CPU allocation set to always allocated (`--no-cpu-throttling`).
   D. Lower the container request timeout to 1 second so requests execute sequentially.

3. You need to deploy an image-processing service from an Artifact Registry container image with 4 GiB of memory, 2 vCPUs, and a limit of 40 simultaneous requests per instance. Which `gcloud` command applies these configurations correctly?
   A. `gcloud run deploy img-proc --image us-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/repo/img:v1 --memory 4Gi --cpu 2 --concurrency 40`
   B. `gcloud run deploy img-proc --image us-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/repo/img:v1 --ram 4096M --vcpus 2 --threads 40`
   C. `gcloud run deploy img-proc --image us-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/repo/img:v1 --memory-limit 4GiB --cores 2 --max-requests 40`
   D. `gcloud run deploy img-proc --image us-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/repo/img:v1 --size 4Gi-2cpu --concurrency-limit 40`

4. When deploying a service with default settings in Cloud Run, how do CPU and memory allocations behave during periods of zero traffic?
   A. Memory stays allocated and billed to keep instances warm, but CPU drops to 0% utilization.
   B. Cloud Run scales instances down to zero, meaning no CPU or memory is allocated or billed when there are no requests.
   C. CPU and memory remain permanently provisioned as long as the deployed revision is active.
   D. The CPU is throttled down to 0.1 vCPU and memory is swapped to disk, incurring a reduced baseline fee.

**Answers**

1. **B** — Concurrency defines the maximum number of simultaneous requests sent to a given container instance before Cloud Run spins up additional instances. Option A is incorrect because the upper limit on the total number of running containers is governed by `--max-instances`, not concurrency.
2. **A** — Setting concurrency to 1 ensures each container instance handles only one request at a time, preventing race conditions while allowing Cloud Run to scale horizontally by spinning up new instances for other incoming requests. Option B is tempting because it restricts capacity, but setting `--max-instances 1` limits the entire service to one single container for all global traffic, which creates a severe bottleneck rather than solving per-instance concurrency.
3. **A** — The standard Cloud Run flags for configuring resources and request multiplexing are `--memory`, `--cpu`, and `--concurrency`. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because flags such as `--ram`, `--vcpus`, `--cores`, and `--max-requests` are not valid Cloud Run deployment parameters.
4. **B** — Under the default request-based billing model, instances scale down to zero when idle, meaning instances terminate and you pay nothing for CPU or memory when no requests are being processed. Option A is tempting because idle container instances can briefly be kept warm before termination, but Cloud Run does not charge for idle memory unless the "CPU always allocated" option is explicitly configured.
